Please read this carefully:

<document>
# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

</document>
response:
This comment does valuable work in its first five sections and then overreaches in the last three. The forensic re-analysis is mostly sound and confirms, with the microdata, several problems that could only be suspected from the Halden working paper. But the conclusion that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact" is not supported by the comment's own numbers. Getting there also requires leaving out half of the Varden trial.

## What holds up

**Attrition (§1) is the most important finding, and it is a reporting problem, not just a bias.**
The working paper said nine organisations withdrew "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons." The microdata show something different:
- Seven of the nine withdrew *after the reduced schedule began*.
- Six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason.

If this is accurate, the original description of attrition was wrong in a way that flattered the result. That deserves a correction from Halden, separate from any question of interpretation.

**The output measure (§2) is well executed.**
The authors compare manager-reported and record-based output within the same 23 organisations. The manager index was higher in 19 of the 23, a gap of 3.8 points. This is direct evidence for the bias that could only be suspected before. The tone ("we do not suggest bad faith") is right.

**Hours (§3) and revenue (§4) check out.**
- 98.4 / 0.859 = +14.6%.
- 95.1 / 0.8 = +18.9%.
- 95.4 / 86.1 = +10.8%.
- 34.6 / 40.3 is a fall of 14.1%.
- 1.014 / 1.041 is a real fall of about 2.6%.

All Table 2 figures reproduce.

**The sectoral critique (§5) is correct.**
Any index above 80 shows a per-hour "gain," so "found in every sector" is built into the method. The retail figures and the Varden counter-office stratum support the narrower claim that output falls where it depends on presence.

## Problems

**1. The abstract says attrition was corrected, but Table 2 doesn't correct for it.**
The abstract states that "correcting the first three" problems, including attrition, brings the gain to 10.8%. Table 2 corrects only output and hours. Attrition is still uncorrected, and its likely size is never estimated.

A rough bound is easy to get. Suppose the nine withdrawers had *zero* per-hour gain and were similar in size to the rest. The average across all 70 would then be about 10.8% × 61/70 ≈ 9.4%. Even assuming the withdrawers lost 10% per hour, the average stays well above zero. Attrition matters, but it cannot by itself remove the remaining gain. The authors should report bounds like these.

**2. The hours breakdown doesn't add up.**
The logs show four longer days (+0.7 hours each, so +2.8) plus 1.6 hours logged on the day off. Added to 32 scheduled hours, that gives about 36.4 hours per week, but the reported average is 34.6. Either the components don't apply to everyone (staggered schedules, part-timers, an averaging artefact) or one of the figures is wrong. It's a small point, but the hours correction is central to the argument, so it should reconcile.

**3. The novelty argument (§6) rests on a two-point extrapolation from the wrong variable.**
- **The extrapolation.** Energy is at +0.61 SD at month three and +0.29 SD at month six. Two points cannot tell a decline that will reach zero apart from one that levels off. Even taken at face value, the straight line hits baseline at around month 8.7, not month ten.
- **The wrong variable.** Self-reported energy is not output. The argument assumes per-hour productivity follows energy, and never tests this.
- **A direct test was available and not run.** The output index was collected *monthly*. If novelty drives the gain, per-hour output should fall between month three and month six in the microdata. The authors have the data to check, and should.
- **A factual slip.** "A change that staff chose" is wrong for Halden. Participation was voluntary at the level of the organisation. All staff in participating units moved to the new schedule.

The authors also concede that "six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one." That is the correct position. It supports "durability is unproven," not "the gain is novelty."

**4. The Varden trial is cited selectively.**
§5 calls Varden's counter-office result "the most reliable finding in the literature." The comment does not mention Varden's case-processing result from the same trial. That stratum is randomised, uses record-based output and timesheet hours, and analyses all units. It meets every standard the comment's own recommendations set. It found **+12.5% output per actual hour (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4) at nine months**, compared with a control group that also knew a trial was under way. Even the counter stratum showed +6.7% per actual hour.

A claim that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact" has to deal with that evidence, and the comment does not.

**5. The meetings section (§7) attacks a claim Varden didn't make.**
Varden's authors themselves said the analysis was unregistered, based on seven offices, and "cannot establish a mechanism." They also registered a confirmatory test. Saying they "suggest this as a mechanism" misstates them. "Selected for analysis after the results were known" is also doubtful: the calendar data were collected in month six, at managers' request.

The better criticism, which the comment misses, is that Varden measured meeting *levels* only in month six. So "offices that cut meetings most" can't be established from their data. "Unconfirmed, awaiting the registered test" is the fair stance. "Should not be cited" goes further than the evidence supports.

There is a further problem for the comment's own argument. The meetings hypothesis competes directly with the novelty explanation. If gains come from removing standing meetings, they are structural and would not fade with novelty. Halden managers raised exactly this point: 47 of 58 mentioned meetings. The comment dismisses the one mechanism that would undercut its novelty argument without weighing it.

**6. The conclusion goes beyond the paper's own data note.**
The data note correctly says the corrected estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole." The conclusion then generalises to "reduced-hours schemes" as a class. There are also no confidence intervals anywhere. The 10.8% estimate rests on 17 non-random organisations and needs one.

## What the evidence now supports

Taken together, the two independent sources agree more than either paper admits:

| Source | Design | Output / hours basis | Per-actual-hour gain, non-coverage work |
|---|---|---|---|
| Halden, corrected subset (17 orgs) | Uncontrolled, survivors | Records / time-tracking | +10.8% |
| Varden case-processing (7 v 7) | Randomised | Records / timesheets | +12.5% (6.9 to 18.4) |

A defensible synthesis:
- **Coverage-bound work.** Reduced hours lower output per employee and worsen service.
- **Non-coverage work.** There is a modest per-hour gain, probably around 10%. This is about half of what uncontrolled pilots report on scheduled hours.
- **Open questions.** Whether the gain lasts is unknown. Whether it comes from rest or from cutting low-value time like meetings is unknown. Neither is settled in favour of novelty.
- **Caveats on both estimates.** Both probably overstate the gain somewhat, because of unlogged or unclaimed work. Halden's also carries attrition bias.

## Suggested revisions to the comment

1. Keep §§1–5. Add the attrition bounds, reconcile the hours breakdown, and give confidence intervals.
2. Test novelty directly using the monthly output data, or downgrade §6 to "durability not established."
3. Report Varden's case-processing result alongside the counter result.
4. Correct the characterisation of Varden's meetings claim, and replace "should not be cited" with "unconfirmed."
5. Replace "entirely an artifact" with what the evidence supports: the reported gain is substantially overstated, and roughly half survives correction in the subset where correction is possible.

There's a pattern across this sequence of documents. Halden overclaimed. This comment, correcting hard against that, lands on the opposite failure: treating a gain that is real but smaller than claimed as nothing at all. That is the "failures come in pairs" problem from your first document, though in this case the corrective lies in the evidence, not in deferring to anyone.

I can draft a short reply to the comment if that's useful, or a synthesis note covering all three reports.
